title: How a Normal Switch Sticks On

scenes.visual: Deep slate (#0F172A) cross-section of a schematic cell slowly fading in with gentle ambient particle drift: a cool slate-blue (#60A5FA) signalling switch at the membrane, an activity gauge at the right, and a two-copy chromosome rack glowing softly along the bottom. Title 'How a Normal Switch Sticks On' appears cleanly across the upper center, then fades out.

scenes.tts: A chicken virus causes cancer using a gene healthy birds already carry. How does a cell's own switch get stuck on, and how many copies does it take? Let us watch one growth switch inside a single cell to find out.
scenes.caption: A chicken virus causes cancer using a gene healthy birds already carry. How does a cell's own switch get stuck on, and how many copies does it take? Let us watch one growth switch inside a single cell to find out.
scenes.visual: Same schematic cell fills 70% of the frame. A small schematic virus badge beside the membrane flashes an amber-gold (#F59E0B) gene strip that visually matches one glowing band on the cell's own chromosome rack below. A pulsing question mark hovers beside the membrane switch as the camera settles smoothly onto the pathway.
scenes.narration: A chicken virus causes cancer using a gene healthy birds already carry. How does a cell's own switch get stuck on, and how many copies does it take? Let us watch one growth switch inside a single cell to find out.

scenes.tts: A healthy cell divides only when told to. Every growth pathway therefore uses an on-step and an off-step. A growth signal flips the switch on. When the signal leaves, an off-switch flips it back off. A normal gene of this kind, able to become a cancer gene when altered, is a proto-oncogene.
scenes.caption: A healthy cell divides only when told to. Every growth pathway therefore uses an on-step and an off-step. A growth signal flips the switch on. When the signal leaves, an off-switch flips it back off. A normal gene of this kind, able to become a cancer gene when altered, is a proto-oncogene.
scenes.visual: Inside the carried cell world, a schematic growth signal dot docks at the membrane switch. The switch lights amber-gold (#F59E0B) and the activity gauge on the right rises smoothly; when the dot drifts away, an emerald-teal (#10B981) off-switch sweeps in and resets the switch to cool slate-blue (#60A5FA) as the gauge drops back to baseline. The label 'Proto-oncogene' lights on the chromosome band below.
scenes.narration: A healthy cell divides only when told to. Every growth pathway therefore uses an on-step and an off-step. A growth signal flips the switch on. When the signal leaves, an off-switch flips it back off. A normal gene of this kind, able to become a cancer gene when altered, is a proto-oncogene.

scenes.tts: Surprisingly, cancer genes are rarely foreign invaders, but altered copies of the cell's own genes. Take the signalling kinase called sark. Normally a phosphate sits on its tail. Another part of the same protein grips that phosphate, holding the kinase shut. Replace that tail, and the grip has nothing to hold. The kinase runs all the time, and that altered gene copy is an oncogene.
scenes.caption: Surprisingly, cancer genes are rarely foreign invaders, but altered copies of the cell's own genes. Take the signalling kinase called Src. Normally a phosphate sits on its tail. Another part of the same protein grips that phosphate, holding the kinase shut. Replace that tail, and the grip has nothing to hold. The kinase runs all the time, and that altered gene copy is an oncogene.
scenes.visual: The switch morphs smoothly into a schematic Src kinase block (cool slate-blue, #60A5FA) held shut by an emerald-teal (#10B981) tail segment whose phosphate dot is gripped by another part of the same protein, labelled 'Phosphate gripped, kinase shut (schematic)'. The tail segment snaps off and turns dashed grey (#64748B) with a crimson break (#EF4444); the kinase jaws spring open, turn bright amber-gold (#F59E0B), and drive the right-hand activity gauge high. The chromosome band below shifts from blue to amber-gold and relabels 'Oncogene'.
scenes.narration: Surprisingly, cancer genes are rarely foreign invaders, but altered copies of the cell's own genes. Take the signalling kinase called Src. Normally a phosphate sits on its tail. The kinase runs all the time, and that altered gene copy is an oncogene.

scenes.tts: A second switch jams differently. Ras is on while it holds G T P. It turns itself off by breaking that G T P down. A helper protein called a G A P triggers the breakdown. One changed amino acid gets in the helper's way. Ras then breaks its G T P down only slowly, even with a G A P, so it stays on.
scenes.caption: A second switch jams differently. Ras is on while it holds GTP. It turns itself off by breaking that GTP down. A helper protein called a GAP triggers the breakdown. One changed amino acid gets in the helper's way. Ras then breaks its GTP down only slowly, even with a GAP, so it stays on.
scenes.visual: In the same switch slot, the block reshapes into a schematic Ras protein holding a glowing amber-gold (#F59E0B) GTP token. First, an emerald-teal (#10B981) GAP helper docks and flips the token off, cooling Ras to slate-blue (#60A5FA). Then a single crimson pin (#EF4444) appears on Ras's docking face; the emerald GAP bounces off, the GTP token stays locked, and Ras glows steadily amber-gold while the gauge rises.
scenes.narration: A second switch jams differently. Ras is on while it holds GTP. It turns itself off by breaking that GTP down. A helper protein called a GAP triggers the breakdown. One changed amino acid gets in the helper's way. Ras then breaks its GTP down only slowly, even with a GAP, so it stays on.

scenes.tts: Now count the gene copies. You carry two copies of nearly every gene, one from each parent. Alter one copy of Ras, and its protein signals nonstop. The normal protein from the other copy cannot turn it off. That is a dominant gain of function.
scenes.caption: Now count the gene copies. You carry two copies of nearly every gene, one from each parent. Alter one copy of Ras, and its protein signals nonstop. The normal protein from the other copy cannot turn it off. That is a dominant gain of function.
scenes.visual: The bottom chromosome rack rises slightly into focus, showing two parallel Ras gene bars ('Copy 1' and 'Copy 2'). Copy 1 stays cool slate-blue (#60A5FA) and sends up normal Ras blocks that turn off promptly; Copy 2 flashes amber-gold (#F59E0B) with a crimson pin and sends up stuck-on Ras blocks that keep the right-hand activity gauge pinned high (labelled 'Schematic'). Label '1 altered copy -> Dominant gain' appears cleanly.
scenes.narration: Now count the gene copies. You carry two copies of nearly every gene, one from each parent. Alter one copy of Ras, and its protein signals nonstop. The normal protein from the other copy cannot turn it off. That is a dominant gain of function.

scenes.tts: There is a second route. Instead of jamming Ras, remove its off-switch, the G A P helper. A gene whose loss lets cells grow when they should not is a tumour suppressor. Suppose a cell loses one of its two off-switch copies. Does the switch stick on?
scenes.caption: There is a second route. Instead of jamming Ras, remove its off-switch, the GAP helper. A gene whose loss lets cells grow when they should not is a tumour suppressor. Suppose a cell loses one of its two off-switch copies. Does the switch stick on?
scenes.visual: Both Ras copies reset to normal slate-blue (#60A5FA). Beside them on the chromosome rack, two emerald-teal (#10B981) bars labelled 'Off-switch (tumour suppressor)' light up, sending a steady stream of emerald GAP helpers upward. One emerald copy then dims to dashed grey (#64748B) with a crimson X (#EF4444), cutting the stream in half. A clear question banner fades in above the switch: 'One off-switch copy lost: does the switch stick on?'
scenes.narration: There is a second route. Instead of jamming Ras, remove its off-switch, the GAP helper. A gene whose loss lets cells grow when they should not is a tumour suppressor. Suppose a cell loses one of its two off-switch copies. Does the switch stick on?

scenes.visual: The question 'One off-switch copy lost: does the switch stick on?' remains clearly visible at top. One off-switch gene copy stays dashed grey (#64748B) with a crimson X while the second emerald-teal (#10B981) copy continues glowing and emitting emerald GAP helpers gently upward toward the Ras switch. A smooth, thin progress bar moves across the bottom edge for 4.5 seconds.

scenes.tts: Usually, no, because one working copy still makes enough helper protein to clear the signal. So the switch stays mostly off; losing one copy stays hidden at the cell level. Only when the cell loses the second copy does the off-step fail completely. That is a recessive loss of function.
scenes.caption: Usually, no, because one working copy still makes enough helper protein to clear the signal. So the switch stays mostly off; losing one copy stays hidden at the cell level. Only when the cell loses the second copy does the off-step fail completely. That is a recessive loss of function.
scenes.visual: The question fades out. Emerald-teal (#10B981) helpers from the single remaining copy reach the Ras switch and turn incoming amber pulses back to slate-blue (#60A5FA), keeping the schematic activity gauge low. Then the second emerald copy ALSO turns dashed grey (#64748B) with a crimson X (#EF4444): the emerald stream stops, Ras stays bright amber-gold (#F59E0B), and the gauge surges high. Label 'Both copies lost -> Recessive loss' appears.
scenes.narration: Usually, no, because one working copy still makes enough helper protein to clear the signal. So the switch stays mostly off; losing one copy stays hidden at the cell level. Only when the cell loses the second copy does the off-step fail completely. That is a recessive loss of function.

scenes.tts: Jamming an on-step needs only one altered copy, because the normal protein from the other copy cannot switch the stuck one off. Removing an off-step usually needs both copies lost, because one good copy still clears the signal. One altered copy jams a switch, while off-switch loss usually needs both.

scenes.visual: The cell frame splits cleanly into two synced mini-panels using the same colour map (labelled 'Schematic'): left panel shows 1 amber-gold (#F59E0B) + 1 blue (#60A5FA) on-switch copy driving a high amber gauge ('1 altered copy'); right panel shows 2 dashed-grey (#64748B) crimson-X off-switch copies driving a high amber gauge ('Usually both lost'), with gentle pulsing signal lines in both.
